issue.title: fix(alerts): Mark query subscriptions whose query can't be built as INVALID_QUERY

labels.name: repo-f814c484
labels.description: Automatically applied to PRs that change backend components

issue.body:
Refs ID-1850

### Problem

`subscription_checker` re-enqueues `create_subscription_in_snuba` / `update_subscription_in_snuba` every run for any `QuerySubscription` stuck in `CREATING` or `UPDATING`. When the subscription's query can no longer be built (an `issue:` filter on a deleted issue, a removed environment, an unknown function, etc.), the task fails the same way on every run and the subscription never leaves its transition status. The subscription consumer already drops results for non-`ACTIVE` subscriptions, so these alerts aren't evaluating anyway. The only effect is a steady stream of task failures (~1.5M events over 14 days across the issues listed below).

### Fix

- Add `QuerySubscription.Status.INVALID_QUERY` (5). It is separate from `DISABLED` so we can count malformed subscriptions without mixing them up with plan-based disabling. Nothing else reads the new status yet; surfacing it in Detector serializers and the UI is follow-up work under ID-1850.
- `create_subscription_in_snuba` / `update_subscription_in_snuba`: if `_create_in_snuba` raises `SubscriptionError` (the query can't be built), set the subscription to `INVALID_QUERY` with `subscription_id=None`, then log and emit `snuba.subscriptions.{create,update}.invalid_query` instead of raising. The update only applies if the row is still in the status the task loaded, so it can't overwrite a concurrent edit or delete. `subscription_checker` doesn't pick up `INVALID_QUERY`. Editing the alert (→ `UPDATING`) or toggling it off and on (→ `CREATING`) recreates the subscription through the normal path.

Skipping the Snuba delete when the old entity key can't be resolved already landed on master in #129955. This PR builds on it.

Snuba HTTP errors (e.g. SENTRY-5WJ6, `HTTP 400 response from Snuba!`) are unchanged and still raise/retry.

### Expected to stop

SENTRY-5SFJ, SENTRY-5WJ7, SENTRY-5XGJ, SENTRY-5WHX, SENTRY-5WJ0, SENTRY-5WJ4, SENTRY-5WJ1, SENTRY-5WJ2, SENTRY-5WJX, SENTRY-5WJY, SENTRY-5WJT, SENTRY-5WJS, SENTRY-5WJR, SENTRY-5WHZ

### Legal Boilerplate

Look, I get it. The entity doing business as "Sentry" was incorporated in the State of Delaware in 2015 as Functional Software, Inc. and is gonna need some rights from me in order to utilize my contributions in this here PR. So here's the deal: I retain all rights, title and interest in and to my contributions, and by keeping this boilerplate intact I confirm that Sentry can use, modify, copy, and redistribute my contributions, under Sentry's choice of terms.

issue.title: feat(api): Add optional endpoint duration budgets

labels.name: repo-f814c484
labels.description: Automatically applied to PRs that change backend components

issue.body:
It's difficult for a team that owns dozens of endpoints to do good latency monitoring.
Each method at each endpoint can vary in how much latency can be acceptable, and it's very easy for rare unacceptable cases to hide in aggregates.

This introduces a new approach: endpoints can specify how slow is clearly too slow, and we report the duration over budget, unsampled, tagged with team and other key metrics.

This means that if an endpoint has some pathological behavior for only a fraction of orgs, and only with certain filters applied, we can easily identify that, and track how severe it is. You can track the aggregate unacceptable user-inflicted delay per endpoint that your team is responsible for. We can also track the rate of unacceptable latency (though that may require additional changes to be doable by-owner).

The real core of this is having a place to encode what we'd count as clearly too slow; it's an odd thing to embed in the Endpoint class vs in monitoring, but maintaining hundreds of values in monitoring configs is notably harder, and expected max latency is a product choice.

In this change, it has only been specified for a fraction of the Issues team endpoints, with a rough attempt to match existing values. Any disagreement with the specific values is valuable product and monitoring discussion, but not directly relevant to this PR.

The end goal here is to be able to set up a Terraform-maintained monitor for this that can automatically direct notification to the owning team, but prior to that we need to see it prove reliable and valuable for Issues team.

I switched to a constant for the 3.0 since repeating the arbitrary value was a bit excessive, and this was if we eventually make the default 3.0 (or whatever) rather than None, it's very clear where we've made a specific choice and where we can use the default.
I also considered having multiple values for different use cases, but defining those would be retrofitting perf standards that we don't really have defined, so I opted not to.

issue.title: feat(action-log): Backfill FIRST_SEEN during derived data regen

labels.name: repo-f814c484
labels.description: Automatically applied to PRs that change backend components

issue.body:
Backfills `FIRST_SEEN` for groups created before it was logged on creation, so one regen sweep (e.g. triggered by a pipeline hash bump) gives every group a first-seen entry.

- `regenerate_stale_derived_data_batch` calls the new `backfill_first_seen_actions` on each batch right before `build_and_promote_batch`, so the rebuild includes the new entries.
- Each entry uses the same idempotency key as the live write, `first_seen:{group_id}`, so it dedupes against live entries and reruns via `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. It's dated at `group.first_seen`, with `SYSTEM_ACTOR` and source `backfill:first-seen`.
- It skips `backfill_actions` on purpose: that invalidates derived data, which would queue another regen for every group. No derived state uses `FIRST_SEEN`, and the batch is rebuilt right after anyway.

The regen only reaches groups that have `GroupDerivedData`. Deploy this at least 7 days after #126942, when every group should either have a live `FIRST_SEEN` or have written an action (and so have GDD). It's temporary: remove it once the sweep is done.

issue.title: fix(api): Validate integer path ids in convert_args

labels.name: repo-f814c484
labels.description: Automatically applied to PRs that change backend components

issue.body:
Follow-up to #128226. Several `convert_args` implementations still pass a string path param directly into an ORM `id=` lookup or `int()`, so malformed ids 500 instead of 404:

- Routes with `[^/]+` (external team details, code mapping codeowners, user notification option details, accept invite `member_id`, `RegionSiloUserEndpoint` `user_id`) raise `ValueError` for non-numeric values.
- Routes with `\d+` (explore saved query, explore formulas, discover saved query) still hit the `BoundedBigAutoField` `assert value <= MAX_VALUE` for out-of-range values and raise `AssertionError`. `UserEndpoint` caught `ValueError` but had the same out-of-range hole.

Each lookup now goes through `to_valid_int_id(..., raise_404=True)`. The exception is the accept-invite endpoint, which already returns 400 for an invalid invite. It uses the non-404 form, so a malformed `member_id` also gets a 400. Regression tests cover each endpoint.

This PR leaves out the endpoints that already catch `ValueError` around the lookup (broadcasts, dashboards, investigations, org repositories, internal app tokens, preprod artifacts). Out-of-range ids can still 500 there, but each fix means touching the existing exception handling, so they're better done separately.
